# Method {#sec-method}

Every loss an ensemble of trees is ordinarily fitted against is a sum of
one term per observation: the correction owed to a given observation
depends on that observation's own error and nothing else. Racing does
not fit this pattern. A finishing order ranks an entire field against
itself — a horse's chance is only ever defined relative to the others it
runs against on the day — so the natural unit is not the horse but the
race, and a single term of the loss has to span every runner in the
field at once. This is the one structural change this paper makes to the
method, and everything else below follows from it.

The likelihood is the one built for paper 2b. Each horse in a race is
given a score by the model, and within that race the scores are turned
into win probabilities by a softmax: a horse's probability is its own
score, exponentiated, as a share of the same sum taken over every runner
still in the field. The finishing order becomes a likelihood by working
down through the placings — first asking which horse won, out of the
whole field; then which horse came second, with the winner now removed;
and so on to the top three, as paper 2b uses — and combining the
probability of each step. This is the Plackett–Luce likelihood, and it
is what the ensemble is trained to maximise (@sec-appx-derivations).
Stopping after the first step, and modelling only the winner, recovers
the conditional logit of paper 1; the likelihood used here is that same
construction, carried further into an ordering of the whole field, as
paper 2b already established.

A score is not a prediction of anything a race result reveals directly,
the way a fitted value in an ordinary regression stands in for an
observable response. It exists only to be compared, through the softmax,
against the other scores in its own race. What the model observes is
which horse won, which came second, and so on, and it adjusts scores so
that the probabilities those results imply move toward what happened: a
horse the current scores under-favour has its score raised, one they
over-favour has it lowered, and the outcomes of many past races
determine, indirectly, what score a horse with a given set of
characteristics ends up receiving. Ability, in other words, is inferred
from results rather than measured directly.

A tree does not need to be told in advance which characteristics
interact. A branch that splits first on which course a race is run at,
and only then, further down, on the horse's stall position, produces a
value that applies only to horses satisfying both conditions — a
particular draw, at a particular course. The effect of the draw is then
free to differ from one course to the next, which is what an interaction
means; a linear predictor can only express this by being handed that
interaction term explicitly, and only for the combinations a modeller
thinks to specify in advance. A tree of depth $d$ can express
interactions among up to $d$ variables this way, discovered from the
data rather than listed beforehand — an advantage wherever a horse's
characteristics are unlikely to combine additively, which every
conditional-logit model in this series has had to assume regardless.

Put together, the space the model works over is partitioned into regions
on which a horse's score is constant, and because every split is a
threshold on one variable at a time, those regions are rectangles
aligned to the feature axes: a horse shares a region with another only
if it matches it on every threshold the ensemble has found, whatever
else distinguishes them. Two horses in the same race will generally fall
in different regions, and it is that difference, carried through the
softmax, that becomes the model's ordering of the field.
